name: Streptococcus salivarius K12
lead: Streptococcus salivarius K12 is a strain of a common oral bacterium sold as an oral probiotic, usually in lozenge form and often under the BLIS K12 name. It is promoted for bad breath (halitosis) and for supporting throat and oral health.[1][2]

The strain produces bacteriocins, antimicrobial peptides called salivaricin A2 and salivaricin B, encoded on a large transmissible plasmid.[3] Researchers proposed that dosing with such strains could crowd out the bacteria that generate malodor.[4] A small preliminary study of 23 subjects with halitosis, published in 2006, examined K12 lozenges after a chlorhexidine rinse regimen.[2]

Safety assessments of K12, including a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind tolerance study, have been published.[5][6] More recent trials have examined other uses, such as oral mucositis during head and neck radiotherapy.[7]

paras: S. salivarius colonizes the mouth and upper airway within hours of birth and is usually harmless, though it rarely acts as an opportunistic pathogen, for example in neutropenic patients.[8] Strains that produce BLIS (bacteriocin-like inhibitory substances) can inhibit other streptococci, including the cause of strep throat.[8]

K12 produces two lantibiotic bacteriocins, salivaricin A2 and salivaricin B.[3] Laboratory work has also reported that K12 dampens innate immune responses in human epithelial cells, including effects on NF-kappaB signaling.[9] Its distribution and persistence in the human mouth have been measured by quantitative PCR.[10] An in vitro and animal study examined K12 against Candida albicans.[11]

A 2006 safety assessment reviewed K12's antibiotic susceptibility, metabolic profile and virulence determinants and examined saliva composition after dosing.[5] A 2011 randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study evaluated its safety and human tolerance.[6]

The 2006 preliminary study gave 23 people with halitosis a 3-day chlorhexidine rinse regimen followed by lozenges of either K12 or placebo, and assessed volatile sulfur compound levels and oral microbiota.[2] It was small and exploratory.

A 2024 randomized controlled trial in the Journal of Clinical Oncology tested K12 for oral mucositis in head and neck cancer patients receiving radiotherapy.[7] Registered trials have also examined K12 for upper respiratory infections in nursery-age children and in COVID-19 inpatients, among other uses.[12][13]

timeline.event: S. salivarius first described by Andrewes and Horder.[8]
Safety assessment and a preliminary malodor study of K12 published.[2][5]
Salivaricin A2 and B genes characterized on a megaplasmid.[3]
Randomized safety and tolerance study published.[6]
Randomized trial in radiotherapy-related oral mucositis published.[7]

card.summary: A bacteriocin-producing oral probiotic sold in lozenges for bad breath; the breath evidence is one small preliminary study.
card.note: Breath-specific human data is a 23-person preliminary study; larger trials target other conditions.

quick.overview:
S. salivarius K12 is a naturally occurring mouth bacterium strain sold as a probiotic lozenge, often branded BLIS K12. People interested in breath use it to try to shift oral bacteria away from odor-producing species.

The breath evidence is a small 2006 preliminary study of 23 people. Larger, newer trials have focused on other outcomes such as oral mucositis in radiotherapy.
quick.mechanism: The strain makes antimicrobial peptides, salivaricin A2 and B, and lab studies report it dampens some epithelial immune responses and persists in the mouth after dosing.
quick.risks: Published safety and tolerance studies, including a randomized double-blind trial, exist. S. salivarius as a species can rarely cause bloodstream infection in people with very low white blood cell counts.
